x: Game values are the shared numbers your game and your server both read: tuning constants, named groups such as combat , and typed tables such as weapons . You author them once. The editor Sync Tool or the owner console stores them on your server, the game reads them with one call, endpoints read the same numbers when they check a claim, and every published build keeps the values it shipped with. This page covers authoring, reading them from the game, using them in endpoints, how they follow published revisions, and a worked example that checks a combat result on the server. For the owner console screens, see admin panel guide . # What a game value looks like A project has two kinds of shared data: Groups are named sets of key and value pairs. combat can hold zombie_hp_per_level: 20 . Endpoints read a group value as {{values.combat.zombie_hp_per_level}} . Tables are lists of rows with typed columns. Each column is string , number or boolean . A weapons table can hold one row per weapon. Endpoints find a row with a lookup or lookup_many step that uses source: values . Game code gets both in one response. The game cannot write game values. # Authoring There are three ways to author game values. The owner console and the management API are the verified paths on release 0.5.4. The current source also compiles Sync Tool YAML game_values collections; release 0.5.4 does not include that fix. x: Network Storage source authoring treats YAML as source code for collections, endpoints, reusable logic, tests, and libraries. The backend compiler is the source of truth: local tools validate early, then sync.py --sources asks the backend to canonicalize and safely upgrade each source before upload. # File Names Local projects store source files in the matching resource folder: Prefer .yml for new files. .yaml is accepted. Typed names are preferred, but plain names inside the correct folder are supported for backwards compatibility. # Endpoint Exposure The new model uses one resource kind for callable logic: kind: endpoint . Use exposure to choose how it is used: Exposure Meaning Client call public Publicly accessible game API endpoint NetworkStorage.CallEndpoint( slug ) internal Reusable Logic, private to backend endpoint/workflow calls not directly callable by clients Public endpoints can still be called internally. Internal endpoints are reusable logic only. # Flat And Wrapper Layouts New source should be flat: resource fields live at the top level next to sourceVersion , kind , and id . x: Endpoints can be written in YAML (steps) or in JavaScript / TypeScript (code). Collections stay YAML. More languages are planned; YAML endpoints are unchanged and stay supported. Code endpoints. Set runtime: javascript or runtime: typescript and put the code in script . The server runs it against the same records, game values, access rules and clock that YAML endpoints use. A full global environment. Any endpoint can be scope: global : it gets no HTTP route and shares its exported functions, classes and constants with every other script, via import { x } from globals/ id or globals. id .x without an import. Existing YAML workflows are callable as workflows. name (input) . Sandboxed. Scripts run inside the server in an isolated interpreter with no file system, network, process or .NET access, and with per-request limits on time, statements, memory, recursion and storage operations (see Limits ). One project s scripts cannot see another project s data. Available on main now and in the next server release (0.5.5). Starting templates for both runtimes are listed at the end of this page. # Contract The script exports a default function handle(req, ns) . Its return value is the response body as JSON. Return plain data (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null). A script ends the request with an error through ns.fail . A failed request answers with its status and this body: The script cannot catch ns.fail . Its status must be in the 400-499 range; the default is 400. # req

x: This guide covers installing, configuring, running, backing up and updating sbox Network Storage Server. For every configuration key see configuration.md . To connect your game see client-setup.md . Status: early preview. Releases before 1.0 may change configuration and storage formats. Keep backups. The local-owner dashboard manages projects, API keys and core settings; it does not yet have full managed-dashboard or managed project export/import parity. Resources can be pushed from the s box editor Sync Tool. # Requirements Linux (x64 or arm64), macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel) or Windows (x64) No .NET runtime needed: release binaries are self-contained SQLite needs nothing extra. PostgreSQL 13 or newer if you choose it. A port reachable by your players (8080 by default) # Local owner and management dashboard Run sbox-ns setup to choose the database and optionally create the owner with hidden password input. Leave the owner username blank to use browser setup. For scripted setup, supply --admin-username NAME --admin-password-file FILE or NS_ADMIN_USERNAME and NS_ADMIN_PASSWORD ; passwords are never accepted as command-line arguments. Password files are read relative to the current working directory, with a final newline removed. Passwords must be 12–1024 characters. Setup retains an existing account rather than overwriting it. For a remote server, the simplest first login is sbox-ns admin login-link . Run it on the server and open the printed single-use link; with no owner yet

h: Player-hosted | Dedicated | Hybrid | Key rules | Self-hosted or managed
x: s box Network Storage is the central server your game is missing. Your game servers, whether a player s listen server or your own dedicated box, are thin callers: currency, XP, levels, items, high scores and every other important rule run here, behind the HTTPS endpoint you control. # Player-hosted A player runs the listen server from their own game. That server only ever holds the public key ( sbox_ns_... ), so it can read shared data and call public endpoints, but every important check runs on this backend. Game collections stay endpoint-only, so a compromised host cannot rewrite player data directly. This is the cheapest way to start, and it is safe by default. # Dedicated Your own box runs the game server with a secret key ( sbox_sk_... ). It can call dedicated-only endpoints ( requiresSecretKey ) and use the management API. Players still only hold the public key in the published game. Use this for tournaments, seasons, or anything worth protecting. # Hybrid Players host day-to-day sessions while your dedicated box handles special modes. One project serves both at once: public endpoints for everyone, secret-key endpoints for your box. # Key rules The game client and any player-run host get only the project ID and the public key. The NetworkStorage.Configure line in game code uses those two values plus your base URL. x: sbox Network Storage Server reads its settings from a folder of commented TOML files. sbox-ns setup writes these files for you; this page documents every key so you can edit them by hand. Changes apply after a restart ( sbox-ns service restart , or stop and rerun sbox-ns start in the foreground). # Owner administration security The owner panel is enabled by default. sbox-ns adminpanel disable writes adminpanel.enabled = false ; restart the server to deny all owner controller endpoints, including setup, login links, login and the dashboard. Game APIs and health remain available. Restore with sbox-ns adminpanel enable or sbox-ns config set adminpanel.enabled true , then restart. Environment and conf.d overrides still take precedence over the file changed by the CLI. adminpanel.demo_read_only defaults to false. It is only for a dedicated public demonstration using an isolated SQLite database: the server seeds fixture data and supplies an ephemeral guest dashboard, rejecting owner auth/security/export, game operations and writes. Never enable it on a real operator database. adminpanel.allowed_ips is an optional comma-separated list of addresses or CIDRs, for example 127.0.0.1,::1,192.0.2.0/24 . An empty string permits all addresses. Restrictions apply before authentication and CSRF to every owner controller route. The policy uses only trusted Connection.RemoteIpAddress and never reads raw visitor headers. The server s existing forwarded-header middleware trusts only loopback prox

x: sbox-ns stores everything in one of two backends, selected by database.provider in database.toml ( sqlite or postgres only). Check the connection with sbox-ns db test and inspect versions with sbox-ns db status . Every key below is also listed in configuration.md . # Which one to choose Backend Choose it when Scaling note SQLite (default) Solo dev, a single server, or first install. Nothing to install or configure. One file, one writer machine. Fine for most single-server games. PostgreSQL 13 or newer You already operate Postgres, want the database on a separate machine, or want your provider s managed backups. Tune the pool (below). One server instance per schema; see below. ScyllaDB is not supported by this server. There is no ScyllaDB provider setting. ScyllaDB notes elsewhere in this repo describe the managed service internals, not this binary. # SQLite Everything lives in data dir /sbox-ns.db (WAL mode). No users, no passwords, no server to run. Copy the file only while the server is stopped; for live backups use sbox-ns db backup , which backs up consistently while running. Each connection opens with journal_mode=WAL and synchronous=NORMAL . WAL keeps committed transactions atomic across an application crash; NORMAL avoids a disk sync on every commit. An OS crash or power loss can lose recent commits, so use reliable local storage and keep backups. # PostgreSQL Connection fields: host , port , database , username , plus either password or password_file . x: Media uploads let a game store small images (PNG, JPEG or WebP) on the server through single-use upload grants. Media is off by default for every project. While it is off, the media routes answer exactly what an unrecognized Network Storage route answers today, so enabling the feature in a build changes nothing for projects that do not turn it on. # Enabling Turn on the server-side backend in server.toml (see configuration.md ). The default is local disk. In the owner panel, open the project s Settings → Media uploads section, tick Enable media uploads for this project , and configure at least one purpose: a name ( a-z , 0-9 , - , up to 32 characters), Enable this purpose , and the limits described below. The project settings are stored under the media key of the project. The owner form rewrites only the purpose named in the form; other purposes are kept. # Flow A grant is a signed, short-lived token. It can be used once; the second upload with the same token gets 409 GRANT_USED . # Routes Each route is also served under /api/media/... through the API root aliases. uploadUrl in the grant response uses the /api/ form. x: Game logs are structured events your game sends to the server, stored per project and searchable by the project owner or a tool holding a log-reading key. They are off by default for every project. While a project s game logs are off, /api/game-logs/{projectId} answers exactly like any unknown route ( 404 NOT_FOUND ). # Turn them on Open the project in the owner dashboard and expand Game logs : Game logs enabled : master switch for the project. Streams : each stream has an enabled flag, retention in days (1-3650) and sampling (0-1, the fraction of entries kept). Allowed client events : comma- or newline-separated event names that public-key callers may send. Names ending in .* match a prefix. Rate limit : entries per minute for the whole project (default 12,000). # Streams and retention defaults Stream Default Retention Who writes it default on 30 days Game events. audit on 365 days Admin and audit events. chat off 14 days Chat messages. Opt-in: nothing is captured until the owner enables it. Entries older than the stream s retention are purged once a day. Search never returns entries older than retention, even before the purge runs. Disabling a stream stops new writes; its stored rows are kept until they age out (purging on disable is not implemented yet). Rows of a deleted project are removed by the same daily purge, under the default retention. # Sending entries A key in the query string ( ?apiKey= ) is refused with 400 API_KEY_IN_QUERY before any key lookup. x: Installable server modules: starter kits (economy, progression, inventory, leaderboards), integrity monitoring (server-side anticheat) and player insights (analytics). Modules are declarative bundles compiled into the binary : a manifest plus authored definitions. They never download code at runtime and never run outside code. # Lifecycle Catalog. The dashboard Modules page lists every embedded module with its version, description, requested permissions, the definitions it adds, and its install state. Works offline; modules.json absent means nothing is installed. Preview. Installing first shows every definition and permission. Name conflicts with existing definitions are listed and the install refuses until they are resolved. Install. Definitions are written into the live definition tables with a module ownership field under the module s id_ prefix (for example economy_earn ). The install is audited and shows a toast. Kit endpoints are public-key callable, so they work in player-hosted projects. Disable. Hooks stop, panels hide, and the module s endpoints answer ENDPOINT_DISABLED . Data and settings are kept; re-enabling restores everything without data loss. Uninstall. Requires typing the module id. Keep data converts definitions to ordinary project definitions (ownership stripped, names and records kept); delete data also removes the module s definitions, its records (ledger entries included) and its game-values items. Definitions outside the module s namespace are never to

Both are owner-only operator diagnostics. They are never exposed on game-facing routes, and the read-only demo does not serve them. No configuration is needed and nothing is sent anywhere unless you add a channel. # Server page The header shows the version, uptime, .NET runtime, OS and architecture, database provider, version and ping, and the data folder. The live tiles update every 500 ms by default. Pick 250 ms, 1 s, 2 s or 5 s, or pause; the choice is remembered in the browser. Each tile has a sparkline of the last 2 minutes, or of the last 15 minutes or 24 hours (one point per minute) when you change Chart . Polling pauses while the browser tab is hidden. Without JavaScript the page shows the latest sample; refresh it to update. x: sbox-ns notifies operators through channels : email over SMTP, Discord webhooks, and generic HTTP webhooks (with presets for Slack-compatible webhooks, Microsoft Teams, ntfy and Gotify). Alerts come from two sources: Captured errors , built in and always on (below). Alert rules you add in the owner console under Alerts , for example CPU use above 90 % for 2 minutes or free disk below 5 GB . Rules, metrics and the Server page are described in monitoring.md . Every send is best-effort: a failed send is logged, shown in the alert history, and never fails the request or rule check that triggered it. No channel is configured by default, and no outside service is required. # Channels Channels come from two places and are used the same way: Where Kinds Edited with alerts.toml , conf.d/ , NS_ environment variables one Discord webhook, one SMTP target sbox-ns config set , restart to apply Owner console, Alerts → Channels any number of email, Discord and webhook channels the console, live Both appear in the console s channel list; alerts.toml channels are marked and read-only there. Each console channel has: Minimum severity : info , warning , error or critical . The channel receives alerts at or above it. alerts.toml channels receive everything. Scope : all alerts (server-wide), or only alerts about one project. Project-scoped channels receive that project s captured errors only; rules watch the whole server, so their alerts go to server-wide channels. Send test sends a real notificat

x: sbox-ns mcp serves the Model Context Protocol over stdio. Your coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop and others) starts it on your server through SSH, or directly on your own machine. Nothing extra listens on the network, and the agent can do only what that login can do. With it, an agent can set up the server, give you the line for your game, write and validate collections and endpoints, dry-run them, read request logs and errors, and look at player records. Each package sync that publishes a revision keeps an immutable snapshot of that revision s definitions; owners set support rules; the server tells each client what to do and can enforce it server-side (opt-in, off by default). # Publishing flow The editor Sync Tool pushes definitions, then POST /api/manage/{projectId}/package-sync with the new currentRevisionId . When the revision actually changes, the server promotes staged overrides, resets revisionPublishedAt to now (the grace anchor), and writes revisions/{revisionId}.json : the full merged endpoints, workflows, collections, queries and game values plus the publish time. The write is once-only: later live edits never rewrite a snapshot. revisions/index.json records the retained ids, grace starts and owner overrides (ended/extended grace). The Versions page ( /dashboard/projects/{id}/versions ) lists live, in-grace and expired revisions with publish times, distinct players per revision (24h, from heartbeat/request identity sketches) and non-additive schema warnings. # Retention The server keeps live plus the most recent N earlier revisions ( N per project, default 3, range 0-20, set under Project → Revision policy).
